intent: Fix the status-downgrade bug in check_and_enable_services, where a later check assigning status="warning" unconditionally could overwrite the status="error" an earlier check had set — so a genuinely broken service was reported and then silently never repaired.
scope: lib/tests/test_services_units.sh — 7 pinning assertions converted to regression assertions
lib/tests/ — test_services_hosts_fix.sh and test_services_hosts_resolved.sh split out for the 250-line cap; stage_hosts_ok moved into the harness so both files can use it
Non-goal: the 5 sites that were already guarded correctly
changes: All 8 bare `status="warning"` assignments now read `if [[ $status != "error" ]]; then status="warning"; fi`, which is the idiom services_apps.sh and services_browser.sh already used — so this makes the family internally consistent rather than inventing a convention.

The blast radius differs between the two files and only one is load-bearing. services_units.sh reports through report_and_fix, which repairs ONLY on "error", so a downgrade there meant no repair ran at all. services_hosts.sh gates its own repair on `status != "ok"`, so repair still ran; there the bug printed a real error as a yellow [!] warning and understated the summary row.

The three unit checks were the worst case because the is-active check is the LAST status assignment in each function, so it could overwrite any error set above it. In check_periodic_systems that is hosts-file-monitor.service, which sits after three separate is-enabled checks.

verification.evidence: The pinning assertions were rewritten to assert correct behaviour first, and failed: 'disabled+inactive stays an error (want error, got warning)' and 'so the disabled timer IS repaired (no call matching /ran setup_midnight_shutdown.sh enable/)' for all three unit checks.

verification.command: A/B against a simulated broken machine: timer disabled AND inactive, unit files present
verification.evidence: Without the fix: status=warning, repair ran 0 times — the timer stays dead. With the fix: status=error, repair ran 1 time — the timer is re-enabled. Run by reverting only the 4 guards in services_units.sh and restoring them afterwards.

Still byte-identical modulo Date:. This machine has no disabled timer and no missing pacman hook, so the buggy path is not taken here — which is exactly why the fault went unnoticed. The A/B above is what demonstrates the behaviour change, since the live diff cannot.

services_units.sh holds 100.00% (72/72) through the change. services_hosts.sh rose from 86.05% to 93.02% as the new masking cases exercised more branches; the 6 remaining lines are the kcov attribution artifact diagnosed in check-and-enable-services-coverage-2026-08-21.json. services_hosts_fix.sh 97.30% (2 pipeline continuation lines).

verification.command: shellcheck lib/tests/*.sh lib/services_*.sh check_and_enable_services.sh; bash meta/scripts/check_file_length.sh --all
verification.evidence: Zero shellcheck findings, no suppression. No file over 250 lines; the hosts test file needed splitting twice to stay under it.

risks: This deliberately changes live enforcement behaviour: services that previously sat in a warning state without being repaired will now be repaired on the next hourly run. That is the point of the fix, but it means the next run on a machine with a disabled timer will actually execute a setup script rather than doing nothing.

A service whose repair script is broken will now retry every run instead of staying quiet at warning. err_missing_script already logs that case at journal error priority, so it surfaces rather than looping silently.
rollback: git revert this commit restores the unguarded assignments and the pinning tests together, so the suite stays green either way.
After rollback, confirm with the A/B: a disabled+inactive timer should report warning and run no repair.
